question_en:
I am looking for trail maps for a park hiking activity that show a route forming a loop around a body of water while also connecting to another route outside the water area. The attachment is a cropped map image without text.
1. Please identify the park it belongs to and the official Trail Maps page based on the image.
2. The scope includes all sections in the main body of the page that use a map name as the title and directly display a trail map; take the first map under the title for each section. Exclude interactive maps at the top of the page, PDFs that only provide download links, and decorative images.
Among these maps, identify sections that meet the following criteria: a single-color solid-line trail forms a closed loop that completely encircles a lake, pond, or reservoir clearly labeled on the map, and connects outside the water body to another solid-line trail of a different color.
Please provide the names of all map sections that meet the criteria.

Answer format: For Question 1, provide the park name and the link to the official Trail Maps page in text. For Question 2, list the names of all map sections that meet the criteria in text.
answer:
Question 1: Park: Cuyahoga Valley National Park, Ohio; Trail Maps page: https://home.nps.gov/cuva/planyourvisit/trail-maps.htm

Question 2: Kendall Lake Area Trails; Oak Hill and Plateau Trails.

## Step 01 · Use the cropped image without text to find the full map

Action: Use the bends and intersections of the trails combined with background gray blocks as clues for image search. Example query: Cuyahoga Valley Ledges Trail map green brown loop.

Evidence observation: The input cropped image corresponds to a local part of the full Ledges Area Trails map; the park's official website main body provides the same map. The match is based on line topology and background shape, not by directly identifying the gray area as a lake.

Action: First check the legend for solid lines, dashed lines, and water body symbols; trace along same-color solid lines to verify if they truly form a closed loop, then check if the water body is inside the loop, and finally check for connections to different-color solid lines outside the loop.

Evidence observation: A closed loop cannot be formed by splicing two colors or using dashed lines; gray fill is valid only when map text or the legend explicitly identifies it as a lake, pond, or reservoir. Water body edges touching the inner boundary of the loop are acceptable, but those falling outside the loop or crossing out of the closed loop are not.
